What is the pathology of diphtheria?
An exotoxin, and a grey adherent membrane that bleeds when it is removed.
What is the bull neck of diphtheria?
Swelling of the neck from enlarged lymph nodes and oedema, in faucial diphtheria.
What is the main cause of death in diphtheria?
Myocarditis, in the second to third week.
What are the neurological complications of diphtheria?
Palatal palsy (with nasal regurgitation), paralysis of accommodation and neuritis of the limbs.
What is the most important treatment of diphtheria?
Early antitoxin, together with penicillin (or erythromycin) for 14 days.
What are the stages of pertussis?
The catarrhal stage (1–2 weeks), the paroxysmal stage (2–6 weeks) and the convalescent stage.

How does pertussis present in young infants?
With apnoea and cyanosis instead of a whoop.

What are the complications of pertussis?
Pneumonia, apnoea, seizures, subconjunctival haemorrhage, hernia and rectal prolapse.
What is the drug of choice in pertussis?
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1, then 5 mg/kg on days 2–5.
Does an antibiotic shorten the cough of pertussis?
No. It shortens the period of infectivity.
What are the clinical features of tetanus?
Trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus and spasms, in a fully conscious child.

What is the paralysis of polio like?
Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes and normal sensation.
What is the acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance rule?
Any child under 15 years with acute flaccid paralysis is notified, and 2 stool samples are taken 24 hours apart within 14 days.
How does polio differ from Guillain–Barré syndrome?
Polio is asymmetric and comes with fever. Guillain–Barré syndrome is symmetric and ascending, and the CSF has a high protein with normal cells.
